content.p: Armenian Power, usually shortened to AP, began in the 1980s as a defensive street gang of Armenian immigrant teenagers in East Hollywood. By 2011 federal prosecutors in Los Angeles were describing it as an international organized crime group that had grown out of the street. On 16 February of that year more than 70 people were arrested in a coordinated sweep, and in the years that followed nearly every one of the 90 people federally charged was convicted, many of them by plea deals. The case, code-named Operation Power Outage, remains the best documented account of what the group did and how it was organized.

Accounts of the gang's origin agree on its outline and differ in detail. According to court documents the Justice Department cited, the gang took shape in the 1980s in East Hollywood; most members were of Armenian descent, and others came from elsewhere in the former Soviet bloc. LA Weekly wrote that its start was fairly innocent: Armenian high school students, many newly arrived, banded together against aggressive Latino gangs in Hollywood and North Hollywood. A Daily Breeze report from 2010 put the start in the mid-1980s and said the community at first saw the members as vigilante protectors before the group "morphed into a street gang like any other."

Pacific Standard, quoting the Los Angeles Times, said that in 1991 the gang took over the parking lot of an East Hollywood mini-mall and made it a headquarters, intimidating customers and shopkeepers. Authorities then put its strength at about 120. The Hetq account, written by an Armenian-American counsellor, adds that the group first fought for territory and later shifted its attention to money and power.

The tension with Latino gangs was real and sometimes deadly. The Los Angeles Times reported in May 2000 that an Armenian man, Armen Petrosyan, was shot dead outside a deli at Hollywood Boulevard and Kenmore Avenue, the third violent clash between Armenian and Latino young people in Glendale and Hollywood that month. Police said he and his attackers belonged to gangs. The paper's report does not name his gang, and a 16-year-old was booked on suspicion of murder.

The LA Weekly noted that in the 1990s AP had fought a bloody war with Latino gangs in East Hollywood but now answers to the Mexican Mafia, known as La Eme, by "paying taxes" on street drugs and other criminal proceeds. Police Magazine, in a first-person article by a law-enforcement writer, said that in the 1990s Armenian Power members, although not Latino, took part as members of the Sureño alliance in meetings called by the Mexican Mafia. The suffix "13" that gangs add to their names refers to the thirteenth letter, M, for the Mexican Mafia; hence "AP-13."

The Justice Department said evidence at the trials showed that AP leaders worked closely with "thieves-in-law," senior organized-crime figures in Russia and Armenia, and with members of the Mexican Mafia. According to LA Weekly, the rise of AP in the early 2000s can largely be credited to two men, Mher Darbinyan and Paramaz Bilezikchyan, who built a strategic relationship with the Mexican Mafia. An FBI agent told the magazine that Darbinyan became one of the first people "validated" as a member of the Mexican Mafia without being Latino. In return for paying taxes, AP received protection inside California's state prisons.

Prosecutors insisted that AP was not a conventional gang. Reuters quoted US Attorney André Birotte Jr. as saying it had no single leadership cadre, unlike the Italian Mafia, but was divided into cells with their own leaders. The FBI agent Jeremy Stebbins told LA Weekly that AP does not fight over turf; it keeps "hangouts" where members gather and plan.

LA Weekly dated the FBI's heightened attention to a public gunfight. Around 6 p.m. in 2008, more than a dozen men from two organized crime groups fired at each other in a North Hollywood parking lot, then continued shooting from moving cars along Whitsett Avenue. More than 50 shots were fired and two people died. Only one person was charged, and, according to the magazine, law enforcement still did not know exactly what had happened; it was thought to have followed a fraud scheme gone wrong. The FBI concluded that Armenian Power dominated the clash. Although it had known of the group for years, the agency doubled its efforts afterwards, the article said.

The announcement on 16 February 2011 rested on two federal indictments and several state cases. The Justice Department's release said they charged 99 defendants in all, of whom 74 had been arrested. Reuters, citing the same authorities, reported a total of 113 defendants, including more than a dozen charged outside California; the Justice Department release counted the Miami and Denver defendants separately. The release listed 88 federal defendants "linked to Armenian Power": 70 in a Los Angeles racketeering indictment, of whom 29 were accused of joining a RICO conspiracy, and 20 in an Orange County bank-fraud indictment, two of them also named in the first. The Los Angeles County district attorney separately charged 11 in state court. The racketeering indictment was described as having 134 counts in 2011; a Justice Department statement in 2014 called it a 140-count indictment. LA Weekly reported that more than 1,000 officers took part in the sweep.

The investigation began about two years earlier, according to the FBI's Steven Martinez, and used undercover agents, wiretaps and informants. Nine agencies were involved. The Secret Service said its own work on the Orange County case had run over five years.

What the indictments alleged was mostly white-collar. In one scheme, members were accused of secretly installing skimming devices at the registers of 99 Cents Only Stores across Southern California, then making counterfeit debit and credit cards from the stolen data. Prosecutors said this caused losses of more than $2 million. In the Orange County case, members were accused of working with members of African-American street gangs and bribing bank insiders to take over accounts, many belonging to elderly customers, for losses of at least $10 million. The Times reported the US attorney's office estimating that the group's activities had cost victims at least $20 million overall.

The violent side came through kidnapping, extortion, assault and witness intimidation. The FBI release described one kidnapping in which several members seized a victim and forced him to pay a ransom at an auto body shop owned by a member, and an extortion scheme lasting months in which a victim and his family were threatened. It also said two defendants were accused of using smuggled mobile phones to coordinate bank fraud from state prison. Birotte called the group one that "appears willing to do anything and everything illegal to make a profit."

LA Weekly told the story of two men who were preyed on. One, identified only as Victim M.M., was threatened by a member nicknamed Horse, who the magazine said made a threat from inside Avenal State Prison to have the man's wife and young child kidnapped and murdered. After months of extortion demands, M.M. went to the FBI with his father. The agency was already listening to wiretaps and, the article said, used him as a cooperator, providing money for small payments to buy time. He later testified, relocated before trial, and declined to enter federal witness protection.

The other, Sandro Karmryan, who ships cars to Russia, was kidnapped twice according to the magazine; his family paid $50,000 after the first abduction. In July 2009, the prosecutor E. Martin Estrada said, he was seized again in a Van Nuys parking garage and accidentally shot by a friend during the attempt. The kidnappers set a $1 million ransom, and the FBI found him after nearly five days. His kidnappers each received 15 to 30 years. Estrada said AP chose victims such as these because they had no gang ties and might fear the police, and that the violence was aimed at people inside the Armenian community, not at rival gangs.

LA Weekly also reported a breach: in 2012 a clerk's office employee at the federal courthouse in Los Angeles and her husband were arrested, accused of using sealed documents to tip off defendants before their arrests. The woman was sentenced to six months and the husband to almost five years.

By February 2014 Pacific Standard counted 78 convictions from the case, including Andranik Aloyan. Aloyan was found guilty by a federal jury on 11 February 2014 of racketeering conspiracy, attempted bank fraud and other counts; prosecutors said he possessed financial information on more than 75 mostly elderly customers, for accounts worth over $25 million. In August 2014 he was sentenced to 160 months and ordered to pay $3,516,711 in restitution. Eighty-one defendants had by then been convicted or had pleaded guilty, 24 of them to racketeering charges.

Few went to trial. In April 2014 the main defendants, Darbinyan, Arman Sharopetrosian ("Horse") and Rafael Parsadanyan, faced a jury, as LA Weekly described it. Prosecutor Estrada said both sides had reasons: the defendants rarely accept responsibility, and prosecutors wanted the highest sentences on some of the worst targets. Darbinyan was convicted of 57 counts, and Sharopetrosian of three. Parsadanyan was convicted of 14 counts of bank fraud; his lawyer maintained that he had no gang ties and was a business owner caught by "guilt by association."

On 10 November 2014 Judge R. Gary Klausner sentenced Darbinyan, then 39 and from Valencia, to 32 years. The Justice Department said he organized a debit-card skimming operation aimed at 99 Cents Only customers, ran a fraud scheme using fraudulent checks on accounts of elderly customers and businesses, and conspired to extort a member of the Armenian community by threatening the man and his family. He had a previous felony conviction for a 2004 debit-card fraud scheme. By then 87 of the 90 people charged in 2011 had been convicted, two were fugitives, and charges against one had been dismissed.

The Daily News reported in November 2019 that Darbinyan, by then 44, pleaded guilty in June 2019 to 30 counts in a second case to avoid another trial. He was sentenced to nearly 18 years and ordered to pay $170,000 in fines and restitution; his lawyer said he "admits that he did wrong." Sharopetrosian, said the paper, had received 16 years, consecutive to a 25-year sentence in a separate case.

The Daily Breeze reported in 2010 on a separate Medicare fraud network alleged to have sought $163 million, which it linked in general terms to Armenian organized crime and a "thief in law," Armen Kazarian. That case was prosecuted under the name Mirzoyan-Terdjanian Organization, and the article does not call it an Armenian Power operation.

In March 2014 a video appeared of two men firing rifles in Syria, one calling himself "Wino" from Westside Armenian Power and the other "Creeper" of the Sun Valley GW-13 gang. CNN, citing records provided by a Glendale police sergeant, reported that they were Syrian nationals of Armenian descent who had been deported to Syria, one in 2010 and one in 2012, because of criminal histories. The FBI's Joint Terrorism Task Force said it was investigating whether the video posed any threat. The LAPD chief said "gang violence is a form of urban terrorism in Los Angeles, and it's not much of a stretch to go to Syria."

LA Weekly reported that authorities say cultural stigma and the community's silence allowed AP to thrive. The Armenian-American Chamber of Commerce's Los Angeles president said that only a handful of Armenians were engaged in criminal enterprises, and compared generalizations to saying all Italians belong to the Mafia. The Hetq writer, himself Armenian-American, described feeling anger at a report on the gang, and said that young Armenian immigrants often adopt flashy clichés while caught between old and new worlds.
The FBI did not present the case as the end of the group. Stebbins told LA Weekly that someone else would rise to leadership and "create new, better ways to do fraud schemes."
